This was my first hitman game that I played back on my PS4, revisiting on PC was great. There's obviously this circlejerk in the hitman community to hate on this one. I'd ignore all that and just go for it, especially if it's on sale. Probably the most in depth game that lets Agent 47 have some character and not act like a machine the whole time. The voice actor for 47 says this is his favorite game! It's super fun, give it a shot.

You might have heard unsavory things about this game: "very un-hitman-like" or "too trigger-happy" or "dumbed down linearity". Those judgments are not without truth, however it is important to realize that this game isn't intended to be played like traditional Hitman (either Blood Money or Hitman World of Assassinations Trilogy), nor should you try to play it that way.

This game isn't designed to be run with perfection/ghostly stealth mindset: nobody touched, no trace, no items taken. You can do it, definitely, but it's not fun. You know what's fun? Choking guards from behind a corner. Sparta kicking a guy down the gaping yawn of a cliff. Hiding your face right in time when somebody is about to get suspicious. Shooting a guy with your signature silverballer. Watching 47 calmly dead-eye 5 bad guys at once with his DOUBLE silverballers (that's right. you can use 2 pistols at once here, unlike the latest games). 

If you feel like you have to shoot to get out of sticky situation, just shoot. The guns are pleasant to use, it has nice sound design, as well as superb feel to its mechanics, in other words it feels satisfying to shoot. Do not worry, you are not pleasing any clients like in the other Hitman games, you are your own client in this one. Do what you must, utilize your whole improvised arsenal. Metal pipe, H.C. Andersen book, bong, scissors, screwdrivers, everything becomes lethal in the gloved hands of our bald friend. 

The downside is of course the absence of contract mode caused by the server ownership feud that was left unsolved, and the linear nature of the levels means youre doing a lot more of sneaking than assassinating, and levels are divided into many sublevels.

But despite those things, I wish you can enjoy the game. This is after all an action game, and you're supposed to have fun with it. Let go of your hitman-ly conscience, garrote, stab, and shoot your way through Chicago and Hope. 
P.S.: You have to attempt Purist mode at least once. It's a whole different experience.

I actually really like it. i love my little screwed up and flawed videogames that have a strong artistic core and direction and really bold art. just another example of why you shouldnt take everyone elses opinion too seriously. from as far as i can tell this game has either been forgotten or swept under the rug for most people. the thing is is that hitman absolution isnt a bad game by any definition of the word. it plays well, looks and sounds great. has great level design and it is more then the sum of its parts. dare i say this is io interactives best game. yes.

the reason why most games i play have zero impact on me, even if they are fun, is that they either go full art or full game. what i mean by that is that you could have a game that tells a great story and has brilliant commitment to a singular vision and the aim to give the player an experience over mere interaction with systems. the problem with these games is that they are rarely ever benifit from the medium that they are created in. they are usually very mechanically light and have a movie like pace to them. then you have the opposite where gameplay is king and the art usually takes a backseat to pure interactivity. where feedback, rewards and progression become the centre focus other the giving the player any kind of "experience"

these are both great but to me this has always been the fustrating balance this artform had to teeter on. its very rarely where a game can be both game and art, my favorites are allways the one that manages this balance.

hitman absolution is one that manages it. these small levels are so rich with atmosphere and have such a tight and consistent direction. every inch of them has something going on, little stories here and there. little pieces of character. enviromental storytelling in every room. so much effort has been put into characterisation and making this world seem real. the game has such a style to it. it feels almost like an exploitation film. you have all these odd moments sprinkled across the game and it is just a sight to behold. i kept playing to see what weird twisted idea the game developers would come up with next. what depraved, ugly and comicly dark imagery the game would present to me with full confidence.

also, ontop of the game being an incredibly rich package of asthetics. one where every single room feels like it had a mandate to tell some kind of small story or tell you about the world or something. the game dosent forget to be a videogame. hitman absolution is fun to play.

the level design keeps shaking things up. one second your in some sewer section underneath a hotel dealing with gangsters and thugs, then you take the elevator up to find a bunch of hotel rooms that all have unique inhabitants. you sneak onto the window ledge in the rain and scoot by some patrols and onto the fancy top floor with a big dining hall. after you meet the antagonist and he sets the roof of the hotel on fire you escape a nearby library and then make your way (after a helicopter chase) to this hippie activist loft. and after that you are on a train platform and have to find away to get one of the trains back within crowds of communtors and cops searching for you with their flashlights.

that is one mission. one.

the game flows between sneaky tense stealth and brutal gun fights. its this ever switching game of cat and mouse where you never feel fully in control. this seems intentional as the game frequently puts you in positions where your not forced into a gun fight but it is implied that the game will not descriminate or punish you for killing a few guards. and, astheticly, it fits this game well. after a exciting and loud gunfight you hide for a little bit... and then get back to the stealthy sneaky stuff. this is done throughout the whole game. These little pockets of adrenaline charged all out interior warfare sandwiched between the quiet skulking around corners and choking people out behind kitchen cabinets is flawlessly done, best out of any game i have ever played. ever.

I would not recommend this game to many people. certainly not people that are expecting a "normal" hitman experience. this game seemingly dosent even want you to use the disguise mechanic (and i suggest you dont too) since in cutscenes 47 is always in his suit and each level is broken up into smaller pieces in a linear sequence its more about these bespoke stealth challenges rather then this huge sandbox map like the later games. i dont know who i would reccomend this too. im not even sure why i decided to play it in the first place. but im glad i did.

hitman absolution is an absolute piece of work. the focus on smaller, linear levels brings this game a richness and density that you cannot get anywhere else. if i was to describe this game in a single word it would be "bold". everything is bold. the levels are bold. the ideas are bold. the gameplay is bold. the way everything looks and sounds and plays is incredibly bold. so there is my recomendation to you. i either have awful taste in art and videogames or this game is auctualy saying something that makes my brain tickle. this is a cult classic in the making. i have played alot of games and no game is quite like this one. weirdly in my head this game is similar to killer7 or dead rising, kane and lynch 2, cruelty squad and the original portal. a group of games i like to call "they are great but i dont know why / games with lots of interesting artistic and gameplay decisions that somehow come together" 

the only things i think this game suffers from is the mark it was branded with... "blacksheep weird one" and "the one where he is depressed and it looks like arkham city" and also that in screenshots and videos it looks like a typical gruff bald protaganist power fantasy cover shooter thing. sorry but max payne 3 is sitting right there... sadly the reason why hitman absoultion didnt shake the world is because its kinda cringe and comes from an era of videogames trying really hard to be serious and mature. Its a stupid big budget AAA game from the xbox 360 era... but whats so wrong about that anyway. this game pulls it off with so much style its hardly a problem... and its also hardly generic. come for the hotdogs and stay for the fireworks. hitman absolution is way better then you think.

TLDR: if you like weird games (that are auctually fun) as much as i do then that is the only time i would recommend hitman absolution. this game is the roughest of diamonds and is seemingly extremely hard to appreciate and it is not perfect or anything. dont expect a traditonal "good time". expect to have your senses shocked and to be weirded out. this game will make you feel gross and mean. the rest of it will perplex you, arouse you, excite you and everything inbetween

a future cult classic in the making. the spiritual successor to kane and lynch 2. yes that is a statement worth sending someone to the psych ward over

The Black Sheep of the Hitman Series. This game is comparable to Splinter Cell Conviction. Its a good game, but its not a good Hitman game. This entry actually introduced a ton of the cool elements that the newer games are known for, like envriomental kills and being able to use almost anything you find as a weapon. This is also the last hitman game to allow you to use the dual ballers and take human shields. This is also the ONLY Hitman game that gives you a Point Shooting mechanic similar to Splinter Cell. You can mark enemies in a room and clear them all with a push of a button (Kind of like VATS in Fallout). I really like this mechanic, and wish it carried over to the newer games. Sure, its not very stealthy, but in a pinch it gets you out of a tight situation. 

However, the game is missing a ton of features of the previous games. You can not choose your gear - Even after finishing the game. You have to find everything in the level each time. The levels are also not one big map (most of the time) but are instead 3 or 4 little maps that you progress through. The majority of this game is spent running and hiding from the authorities, instead of going after targets. Many levels dont even have a target, making it impossible to get a Silent Assassin rating on them. 

However, there are a few particularly great moments in this game that feel like they are from better installments in the series. The King of Chinatown mission early on in the game feels just like an OG mission. So does the one almost half way through called "The Streets of Hope" where you have  to take out members of a gang. But that's about it. Some of the writing feels extremely cringey, even for the time. Just characters who sound like they were written by a 14 year old who was trying to seem mature. I'm not adversed to coarse words but this game uses them as punctuation. Lots of games from this time were edgy but this one seems like it was trying to win an award.  

I like this game, but its easily the worst in the franchise. IO Interactive tried some new things with this one, and not all of their ideas worked. Thankfully, IO was able to use what did work in this game to bring us the WoA Trilogy, which are easily the best in the game despite some flaws. Recommended with a huge asterisk.

If you want Hitman: ignore the story and enjoy the levels 
If you want a story-main game: don't skip the cutscenes

Absolution draws a hard line between itself and the previous 4 installments of the game without alienating die hard fans of this franchise. Absolution is far more cerebral than it's predecessors. The storyline is multifaceted and weaves together a plot that focuses on exposing 47's ambitions, strengths, and flaws without making him appear weak or whiny; he is still the ultimate badass, but much more human and believable. Absolution shows a more realistic and approachable 47; one I, and I assume others, can easily identify with. This game really develops Hitman's character on a much deeper level than previously attempted.

The movements of 47 are very swift and responsive. In fact, many of 47's movements can be compared to how Sam Fisher's movements are in the Splinter Cell games, which means players can now access cover and look around at a 360 angle. I would also compare the sneaking around to the Metal Gear games, as well. In this game, there are just SO many ways to go about taking out a primary target. On one level, I was given the option to take out a target in 12 different ways. That way could be by taking him out, wearing various disguises, taken him out quietly, poisoning his food, blowing his car up or taking him out with guns blazing. Not to mention, players can get reward for doing so, which enhances the replay value of this game.

The AI has been greatly improved. Characters interact with their environment, situations, and the actions of 47 in many fascinating ways now. Characters generally still have predetermined paths but they can now be interrupted, altered, redirected, and distracted to allow 47 to accomplish his objectives. This really makes a difference in the game play. You no longer have to memorize guards paths or actions, rather you can now change the course of events by affecting the characters in any given situation to gain access to your targets.

All in all this game is by far the best adaptation of Hitman yet. I highly recommend it. You can play this game and still feel comfortable without having ever played any previous versions.

[h1][b]UPDATED 2016: I decided to give this game another chance and began playing it again, however I've been unable to progress at all due to the game or Square Enix servers wiping my campaign progression... TWICE. Therefore, Hitman: Absolution is broken and was shit in 2012, and is still shit in 2016.[/b][/h1]

[h1][b]Summary[/b][/h1]

[b]Wow what happened to this??? Each Hitman game got better & better, but Absolution brings the series crashing down. They tried to breathe new life & add new gameplay features to refresh the franchise: instead it just doesn't work, feels broken, frustrating & hilariously bad.

Kiddie Steam reviewer verdict: 
- wore disguise, disguise blown in 5 seconds, so killed every1. 
- walked past guard, nearly got detected so tilted head low. ran out of power, cudnt tilt head anymore. disguise blown, so killed every1. 
- ran 2 exit, disguise blown. cudnt open exit door cos game wudnt let me, so killed every1.
- Stopped playing game, played agen next day, saves got wiped by square enix server. 3/10 wud NOT play this shit game agen.[/b]

[h1][b] Hitman: Abomination - Problems in the first 5 minutes[/b][/h1]

The trademark disguise mechanic has been drastically altered for the worse. Nick an engineer's uniform, & every single engineer in the country will be able to see through your disguise in mere seconds: it's like they all have an entire database in their heads of what each other looks like. Even if you're half way across a map, partially concealed by a dumpster & have your back to everyone whilst in the shadows, they can still see through your disguise! What the hell??? When you have a series that successfully utilise a unique mechanic that works throughout each game, then you change it so much that it becomes broken & frustrating that you end up just forgetting about it & shooting your way through levels, something has seriously gone wrong.
     The absolute (see what I did there) worse offender of the disguise mechanic is that when you take the clothes of someone wearing a full face mask HE DOESN'T PUT THE FACE MASK ON!!! In all past games, Mr. 47 could hide his face, yet now all of a sudden he refuses to wear anything to conceal his face, like he suffers from an allergic reaction to face cloth. It's no wonder why everyone can spot you through your disguise, seeing as you're the only one wearing a hazmat suit without a gas mask on looking like a prick.
     
Best way to play past the flawed disguise mechanic is to sprint full speed everywhere, hugging walls, hiding behind objects & ninja rolling between cover. It's embarrassingly sad & hilarious that sprinting through the entire level hiding behind things & rolling all over the place like a hyperactive toddler grants less suspicion then walking around the place like a fully grown man would normally do. The NPCs even make remarks like “act like a grown man!” when you start trying to hide. Who would have thought that the game is self-aware.

But this is Hitman: Absolution I’m playing, not Splinter Cell or Metal Gear Solid Absolution, so why the fuck am I rolling all over the place instead of blending in??? Speaking of which, you STILL can get detected when you’re wearing a disguise in a crowd of around 50 people.

[h1][b]Arcade mechanics lead to hilariously bad results[/b][/h1]

New to the series is Instincts mode. Switch it on & time slows down, the background will turn monochrome whilst enemies, their walk path & important objects will glow. Instincts mode also allows you to blend in, such as scratching your head or tipping your hat low to obscure your face as you walk past people. But the problem is using this drains your instincts meter (mana?) so if it runs out, suddenly Mr. 47 loses the ability to simply lower his head again. Seriously??? 
     There are a few select objects in the world that you can use to blend in: this not only recharges your instincts meter, people no longer suspects you of being an assassin. I think I'd be pretty suspicious of a guy constantly mopping a tiny area in front of his feet for a straight 5 minutes or a Policeman inspecting a doughnut like he's counting the individual atoms on it. Did I mention once this meter runs out, you suddenly lose the ability to tip your hat low or scratch your head? Maybe 47 has a stiff neck and the mana metre is actually his muscle fatigue. 

Regardless, these features in the game are so strangely unhuman-like & illogical it's fuckin’ hilarious.

[h1][b]Other flaws[/b][/h1]

Other minor flaws of the game is not being able to choose gear during the campaign, linear missions, ability to hide multiple huge guns and objects in your coat, enemies not noticing you strangling someone to death right next to them, silencers attach instantly to guns, 

[h1][b]Scoring System[/b][/h1]

Because it’s cool and it’s Square Enix, you have a scoring system that rates you on how well (or how shit) you are during each mission. Whilst it’s a nice idea to try to rack up the highest score as possible, it’s frustrating when bad game mechanics hamper this. As you can imagine, I’ve had to shoot my way through most levels, so most of my level score is in the minus thousands region. Anyone want to try to beat my lowest scores, huh??

[h1][b]Light at the end of the rainbow[/b][/h1]

Well, Hitman: Absolution isn’t that bad. It’s just far from good. As a Hitman game, it fails miserably. As a cover based shooter with minor stealth mechanics, it’s decent enough.

[h1][b]Conclusion[/b][/h1]

I brought this for my friend’s birthday sadly, and to this day I still don’t know if he forgives me. Heck, I don’t know if I’ve even forgiven myself.

How can I best summarise this game? It's like that kid at school who boasts about driving an expensive sports car, has the latest £2000 super computer & has 5 different girlfriends. Then one day to his horror, his over-affectionate mum comes to pick him up from school, tells everyone that he stays at home all day playing on his cheap Macintosh & he is scared of girls. Then he goes all embarrassed & tries to stop his mum, only to trip over & his pants fall down in the process, everyone laughs & ridicules him, then they all go away & never look at him the same way again & he is left disgraced & shamed. Hitman: Absolution is that kid.

This game was an unfinished business for me. Blood Money was my first Hitman, then I played Contracts, because it was a good entry point to get to know some classic missions from the first two games. Then I played the new trilogy. The common ground between all those games is essentially one thing: it's a sandbox. You do reconnaissance, you pick your gear, you make your plan and follow it. It's been a signature style for all Hitman games. Except for this one. 

Absolution is different from all the Hitmans I've played. It does not mean it's a bad game. It's pretty stylish in its own way. The shooter part's got much better in comparison with Blood Money. But it's too linear. Except for the tutorial mission, the closest thing to Hitman I know were the Chinatown mission, mission on the arena and a mission in a small town which reminded me "A New Life" from Blood Money. Those three had variety, complex level design and some creative eliminations. I can't say the same thing about the other missions. The developers clearly wanted to experiment and make Hitman more cinematic and add more action to it. Unfortunately, it didn't work on me. 

The stealth part is a mess. There's no point in using a disguise because every enemy of the same rank blows your cover in a matter of seconds, unless you use your instinct to cover your face. But the problem is, in order to restore your instinct, you have to do things like killing or subduing enemies, finding evidence, hiding bodies etc. What if I don't want to mess with this? My favorite way to complete Hitman missions has always been the cleanest way possible with minimal interactions with other NPCs except for the target. Then I end up in a situation where I passed through multiple locations unnoticed and then I have zero chance to replenish my Instinct because the location is packed with enemies I don't want to kill and the other ways to gain instinct are absent. Absolution does not encourage Silent Assassin gameplay. In fact, it does everything for you to fall into shooter at some point. Most of the locations in the game are linear and don't involve more than 1 or 2 ways to pass them. Moreover, since you don't get to choose your gear before the mission, you often have to improvise on the spot. Add the disguise issue I mentioned and you get a stealth game where stealth is inferior to shooter. The final hour of gameplay makes stealth so painful it genuinely gets easier just to shoot your way through to the final titles. 47 can take a lot of bullets in this game, so shooting enemies is much easier than in all other games of the series.

All in all, it's not a bad game by itself. It's not too long, it's got a lot of cutscenes, action parts are fun. But it's not a good Hitman game and if you want to play it like one, sticking to stealth and creative ways of eliminating your target, this one might not be a good choice.

Yeah, I can see why people dislike this game.

While this game does introduce a number of systemic gameplay improvements, most of which carry over into the reboot trilogy, it also makes a number of steps back. It is almost closer to an action adventure game rather than a sandbox assassination puzzle game that every single other entry in the series are.

A lot of levels don't even have anything to do with what a Hitman game is - killing targets unnoticed and in creative ways. Some level sections can be completed in a few minutes without killing anyone, just walking from point A to point B.

Second thing they changed for the worse is the scoring. It's not as bad as the early games, but this game somewhat relies on replaying levels to get Silent Assassin rating on them, if you care about that. You can still do a self-imposed no detections/bodies found runs, basically no negative points runs, but only a few levels can actually count as Silent Assassin without replaying them after doing challenges, which increase the score multiplier. The only good thing is that you know when you screwed up by being spotted, unlike other games.

Then the save system was also changed for the worse. It may be in service of the more linear levels, but you can only save in specific points, and only once per point. This again, like the very first game in the series, severely limits ability to experiment with the game. The save system also doesn't function well as NPC positions are reset on load, and will not appear where they were when you saved.

This game also introduces the issue of accidentally walking into trespass areas voiding your perfect rating, which also also lame. Guards barely try to tell you that you are not allowed to enter some place. This is something that is carried over into the reboot trilogy, and was handled better in Blood Money.

Another regression-y issue is that enemies can see through your disguise from way too far on normal. It makes most disguises kinda pointless, since every NPC in the same disguise can see through your disguise, just a bit slower than with no disguise.

There is a helicopter section where the helicopter can see you through walls if you do not use the cover system, even if you are in the exact same spot but not in cover - it can see you through walls.

The character also turns around exceptionally slowly, making escaping detection that much more frustrating.
There is no map.

Finally, there online-only BS. It started with this game. Contracts mode is now permanently offline, but at least the single player challenges are still available, unlike the reboot trilogy, where even that is locked behind a BS online only requirement. IOI being the worst company that they are. This is the fate of World of Assassination games as well, and they have a LOT more content locked behind a BS online-only requirement, including a lot of single player only content, such as map mastery challenges, scoring and even single player DLCs. I hate IOI.

Overall, I can't say that this game is purely bad, but it makes a lot of strange departures from the previous game(s), which may make the game less enjoyable. It can be picked up on sales dirt cheap though, so I'd wait for sales.

As of 2016, it has been 10 years since the release of Hitman Blood money, the game defined the Hitman style of play and is regarded as one of the best stealth games of all time, to which I agree.
6 years later we now have Hitman Absolution developed by IO interactive and published by Square Enix, is it better than Blood money? or does it fall flat? Let's start with the plot.

Hitman Absolution kicks off right after the Hitman book: Hitman Damnation by author Raymond Benson, which took place after Blood money. Agent 47 (The main character of the Hitman Franchise) is told by the new head of the ICA: Benjamen Travis, to assasinate 47's former handler Diana Burnwood. When 47 shoots Diana, she tells 47 to save a girl by the name of Victoria as her last dying wish. I thought the plot was pretty well done 

Let's get this out of the way first, the game is absolutely gorgeous with highly detailed locations, great lighting, sharp textures, great character models and animations. However, there is a bit too much bloom, especially 47's bald head.

The gameplay mostly consists of you having to get from one end of a level to the other while trying not to get spotted by enemies. Some missions have you killing a certain target within an area and these sections are by far the best parts of the game. You have a variety of ways to kill your target which goes from using electricity, blow up, grind, burn alive, blow up, stab, and yeah you get the idea. If you're not the sneaky type and want to shoot your way through the game's serveral chapers, that is also an option, the gunplay is perhaps one of the most tight I've played in a third person shooter. In each level there is a item you can find called evidence, which can be used to boost your score, and this takes me to the new feature for the Hitman franchise: the points system.

In almost every level, you will be scored on how you completed a level, such as losing points if you had to kill an NPC and didn't hide the body, killed the target in a creative way, lose points when spotted, etc. When you got enough points, you can learn assassin techniques which can be used to make 47 more efficient, such as reducing the time it takes to reload your gun, run faster, more health, and you get the picture. A returning feature is the much loved disguise system since the first Hitman game, although it works a bit different here.

If you find a disguise in a level, you can then wear it and move among the enemy, however it does not shield you fully from the enemy. If an enemy or civilian sees you while wearing their clothing, they will take longer to realize that you don't belong here and will investigate, however the other people in different clothing will not find you suspicious. This new system definitely works in my opinion, and if it was like blood money, the game would be almost impossible to fail.

A new mode to the series is contracts mode, you pick one of the many levels in the game, look around and then mark 3 targets, kill them how you want, and put it online to see who can do the same hit more efficiently. This mode is probably the closest you'll get to Blood Money gameplay and is definitely a mode that shouldn't be avoided. When you complete a contract in contracts mode you earn money which can be used to buy upgrades for your guns, buy disguises, and more guns.

The sound design of the game is top notch, the music is well done even without Jesper Kyd, and the voice acting is superb, especially David Bateson who voices 47 who does an exceptional job.

The A.I. in this game is also pretty good, they will actively search for you if you are hiding and know when to take cover during fire fights. Although there were still parts where they did act strange, such as ignoring dead bodies and shooting in the wrong direction.


In the end, Hitman Absolution is an excellent edition to the Hitman franchise and shouldn't be overlooked just because it's not that much like Blood money. I even think Absolution is just as good as Blood money.

Hitman: Absolution is a stealth game, developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix. This instalment is the 5th game in the Hitman series. The game was released on November 20th 2012; ironically this is the 47th week of the year, referencing the main character Agent 47. 

As with the rest of the Hitman series, you play from a third person perspective. You play as Agent 47 who is the best hitman around. Gameplay is very similar to the previous games, with a strong focus on stealthy progression on every level. At points there will be times where a gun fight will break out, but that usually means you are either very close to the end of the mission or have chosen the path of a deadly mercenary and just going all guns blazing anyway.  Each mission has multiple ways of completing it; you can actually finish the whole game by not shooting anyone, you can set up scenarios so that your “targets” die in an “unfortunate” accident or poisoning.  One of the major changes to Absolution is that Agent 47 now has an “Instinct” ability – this allows you to  track enemies more, and shows up interactable objects more easily. This of course has a limited supply but will slowly regenerate over the course of the mission. The stealth side of the game is done very well, and has the right amount of challenge for you to not get stumped with not being able to progress, but not so easy that you can do it blind folded.  The ability to pick up objects around the world and throw them into enemies path’s to distract them is always a good addition to a stealth game; but also sabotaging items such as electrics to also cause a distraction. The main aim of most of the missions is to take out a target, whilst causing as little disruption as possible, you are scored at the end of each mission taking into consideration how many “non-targets” were killed and other variables. 

Graphically, Absolution is stunning.  So much so that the actual gameplay looks better than the cut-scenes. The animations are perfect both in game and in the cut scenes too; it looks like you are playing a film at times. On top of the gorgeous graphics, the sound effects and voice acting are all perfectly spot on. 

Sadly this game is not as challenging as previous games; this was done to bring in a broader audience to the franchise. You can play the game on a fair few levels of difficulty; hard-core fans of the series will need to be playing this on the harder difficulties. You can always make the game even harder by playing through the game in a complete stealth style. 

All of the Absolution’s missions are huge and extremely well designed. Each of them has more than two ways of completing the objective, on each level there will also be evidence that you can destroy, this will grant you more points at the end of the stage by doing so.  The levels have plenty of buildings, and rooms to explore and you’ll spend most of the time hiding in them to be fair! 

The game is very an extremely good length; it took me just under 28 hours to complete, this was mainly because I tried to complete each level as stealthy as possible, but even then, twenty eight hours for any game is long! There is also a huge amount of replay ability in the game too; not only can you replay the story mode on different difficulties and trying out different methods of taking out your targets, but there is also the “Challenge Mode”, which is player made missions giving an almost infinite amount of gameplay for you to play through. 

I had no technical problems with Absolution, I wasn’t able to push the game out on 4k resolutions, simply because it dropped my frame rate below 60, but that is because the graphics would have been mind-boggling. The game can be played with a controller, but I would suggest playing it on keyboard and mouse as you may need quite a bit of precision when it comes to planning your attacks. The game also has plenty of graphical options which are always nice to see; a field of view option would have been nice though. 

To sum up, Hitman Absolution is in my opinion one of the best Hitman games; nothing will ever come close to being better than Contracts, but this one is easily second to that. The game’s gorgeous graphics, stellar gameplay and Hollywood like plot easily makes this one of the best games of from recent years.  The regular price of £14, 99 is very fair for this game too; however it is pretty much always on sale, so wait for the reduction if you can!

Hitman: Absolution takes a more personal approach than previous entries in the series, following Agent 47 as he questions the orders he's spent his entire life obeying. Beneath the stealth gameplay lies a subtle exploration of morality and redemption. While the game isn't overtly religious, it borrows heavily from Christian imagery and symbolism. Characters often speak in terms of sin, forgiveness, and sacrifice, and the contrast between innocence and corruption is woven throughout the story. Even the Saints—assassins disguised as nuns—serve more as a symbolic commentary on hypocrisy and the misuse of religious imagery than as genuine religious figures.

What makes these themes effective is that they never overshadow the core experience. Agent 47 isn't portrayed as a religious man, but his journey resembles a search for redemption, choosing compassion over blind obedience for perhaps the first time in his life. Combined with cinematic storytelling, satisfying stealth mechanics, and memorable level design, Hitman: Absolution offers a darker, more character-driven experience than other games in the series. It may not be the definitive Hitman game for sandbox enthusiasts, but it's an engaging story that uses religious symbolism to reinforce its themes rather than define them.

Booting up Absolution again feels like stepping into a time capsule of 2012 cinematic gaming taking me back to my high school gaming days. The vibe of this game is unmatched. It doesn't have the clean, sterile, high-society aesthetic of the modern World of Assassination trilogy. Instead, Absolution is drenched in sweat, rain, neon lights, and a deeply cynical, over the top grindhouse film energy. The stylized, high-contrast lighting and bloom effects scream early 2010s in the best way possible. Is it a traditional Hitman game? No. The disguise system is famously broken where every single person in the same uniform instantly detects you unless you burn through your instinct meter. But judged on its own merits as a dark, stylish, linear action stealth thriller, it is a phenomenal experience that they simply don't make anymore.  Lastly, coming back to it feels like visiting an old, chaotic friend. For the pure joy of the atmosphere, the punchy mechanics, and the sheer 2012 nostalgia, it’s a flawless trip down memory lane.

Hitman: Absolution is a game that’s hard to review because, while it offers moments of pure, elegant assassination, it also feels like it took a few steps backward compared to its predecessors. As the fifth entry in the series, it introduces some fresh ideas but also abandons some of what made Hitman stand out in the first place.

What I Liked:
Beautiful Environments: The game’s levels are absolutely stunning. From bustling city streets to dark, atmospheric interiors, the environments are incredibly detailed and immersive. You can get lost in these locations as you plot your next move.

Classic Assassination Gameplay: For all its flaws, when Hitman: Absolution hits its stride, it's still got that signature stealth and strategy that makes the series so unique. Planning your hits, disguising yourself, and using the environment to your advantage is still the core of the experience, and it’s satisfying when everything goes according to plan.

Multiple Approaches: Each mission offers a variety of ways to approach your targets. Whether you want to go in guns blazing, silently pick off enemies, or set up elaborate accidents, the game offers enough options to cater to different playstyles.

Contracts Mode: This mode lets you create your own hit assignments and challenge others, which adds replay value and some much-needed longevity to the game.

What Could Be Better:
Linear Level Design: One of the biggest departures from earlier Hitman games is the more linear structure of the levels. In previous titles, you were free to explore and experiment in wide-open sandbox levels. In Absolution, many of the levels feel more restricted, funneling you down narrow paths that limit your freedom.

Story and Characters: The story feels forced, and Agent 47’s character is oddly less engaging than in previous games. There’s a lot of focus on a personal narrative that doesn't really suit the silent assassin we know and love. The plot also has some odd twists that don’t land well, and the characters feel more like caricatures than genuine threats or allies.

AI Issues: While the AI can be smart and responsive, it’s not always consistent. Enemies can spot you too easily in certain situations, and in others, they’re almost oblivious to your presence. This makes the stealth mechanics feel more inconsistent than they should be.

Less Focus on Pure Stealth: While the game still encourages stealth, there are sections that feel more action-oriented, with shootouts and intense chases. These can break the flow of the more methodical, stealthy gameplay that Hitman fans typically love.

Conclusion:
Hitman: Absolution is a solid game with moments of brilliance, but it doesn’t fully live up to the legacy of its predecessors. The stunning visuals and varied mission options are great, but the more linear level design and awkward story hold it back from being a true classic. If you’re a fan of the series, it’s worth playing, but it’s not the pinnacle of Hitman that many hoped for. Still, there’s fun to be had, especially in the more creative assassination opportunities, and the Contracts Mode keeps things fresh for those who want to make their own kills.

[h1]A SOFTER TAKE ON THE SERIES[/h1]

Agent 47, in all the previous games as far as I can remember was a predator and a highly skilled professional who was literally a ghost, until this game where he is not exactly the legend like the past. While the old games succeeded in creating a sense of dread when Agent 47 was around, this time around we see a soft, humane Agent 47. Perhaps this is because for the first time he is caught up in a narrative, but in all honesty they could have still pulled off the old ambience that made Agent 47 a man to fear. If you ask me, they made him look reckless and amateurish in few parts of the story. Speaking of story, the plot kind of drags on longer than necessary due to someone as ruthless and skilled as Agent 47 fails to eliminate an annoying old guy (one of the antagonists, who isn't even a big timer). That and the roundabout approach in eliminating the said target, together with protecting/saving a girl and countering the Agency's efforts to hunt you down, all of this creates bloated drama- just like in the movies but inadvertently ruining the formidable image of Agent 47.       

Story aside, the gameplay however is immaculate. The stealth system is fluid, the new feature called 'Instinct' adds to realism and the score system for each mission, making you work to complete various challenges on offer to improve your score, contributes to replay value.

Therefore, in terms of gameplay I can say that the game is truly brilliant, with the game giving you plenty of options on how to tackle a scenario and eliminate targets.

There are 20 missions in the game, making it pretty long (30 to 60 hours) depending on the difficulty you choose. Hard might be the go-to difficulty for people who have played the older titles.

The graphics still hold up and does not look dated. Music/Sound/Voice-acting are fine as well. Enemy/AI movement and animations might look stiff. Another notable down-side is you can't unlock all achievements, as online functionality is obsolete as on date.

I didn't expect to like this too much.  It received a degree of negativity on release, and I never really got to grips with Blood Money.  However, I LOVE stealth games and decided to give it a go thanks to sales.  Glad I did!  At this late stage I'm probably preaching to the converted, so this review is aimed at anyone else who couldn't really get into Blood Money either.

[h1]The good[/h1]
The primary reason this title gets attacked is that it's not open-world.  It's not, but the worlds presented to Agent 47 are still pretty large and there feels like 101 different ways to deal with targets.  It didn't feel overly linear like some titles.  There were many different approaches you can take to reach your targets, hiding and sneaking strategies offered, many weapons, distractions and disguises.  There are a whole variety of ways in which to complete your asignments without firing a shot or being anywhere near the victim.  The AI isn't exactly epic but does the job well enough (it's on a par with most other stealth games where the AI patrols their areas in a timed and predictable fashion).  Their narrative was the usual repetitive statements (very much like [i]Dishonored[/i] though perhaps not as bad) and you soon begin to realise that guards aren't saying things because they've actually seen you, but because it is the next line to be spoken in the databank of lines.  Plenty of other games do this too, so that's no biggie.  What the game did well was making many varied people models so there was no feeling of copy-pasted NPCs everywhere.  Crowds were very convincing.  Animations of just about everything was fluid.  The locations were impressive, offering many different routes and places to hide without being overly obvious in their use of props for Agent 47 to use as cover.  Agent 47's use of multiple disguises was a great mechanic and a staple of the series.

Another reason I've seen this title attacked is because it is an 'action' game.  No, it's not, but it CAN be played as an action title if players prefer that and oftentimes it can be easier and all too tempting to play that way, but if you do, you rob yourself of the silent assassin experience that the game achieves so well.  I found it much better to 'role-play' as a deadly, silent and fatally efficient assassin who must not be detected at any cost, and the game offered a much better challenge as a result.  There is a huge range of (often rather similar) weaponry, most of which is arguably redundant if playing the game 'properly' (ie by stealth).  More useful were the number and variety of objects to be used as distractions.  Weapons, when used, were satisfying and the sniper rifle was a joy to use.  Unlike Blood Money, the controls are extremely simple and effective this time.  No more missing with the wire or fumbling around for exactly the right weapon.  Gamepads are fully supported with a properly-working auto-aim for people who want that advantage.  The opening chapter is a very effective tutorial chapter to introduce all the game mechanics you'll use.

The overall stealth aspect of the game is fabulous with a perfect difficulty pitch.  If you enjoy stealth play, this has to be in your library of games!  Although the game felt somewhat short, I was surprised to find it took me around 32 hours to complete the game end to end.  I definitely want to replay it!

Finally, the controls are pure joy!  Much improved over Blood Money's clunky, messy PC controls.  This is an easy game to play - perfect for people without Olympic Gold Medals for gamepad dexterity!


[h1]The bad[/h1]
The game commits the cardinal sin of several 'points of no return'.  Why don't developers understand how game-breaking it can be to have a door closing permanently behind you without warning, with no way to return?  It breaks the immersion, it prevents players from returning for collectibles (more on those soon) and yet they're really not necessary.  Sure, games often need to be semi-linear if we are to be given rich and varied worlds to play in, and a new map needs to be loaded and the old one flushed out of memory, but at least give us some gateway back to an earlier checkpoint within the same chapter even if that does mean a loading screen here and there (similar to the design of [i]Dishonored[/i] where maps would funnel back to one doorway that triggered a reload of the previous area).  As much as people complain about loading screens, they are certainly preferable to denying the player any means of retracing steps if anything has been missed - especially in a game where the player cannot save their progress manually.

The other element I didn't like were many of the in-game achievements.  There were many that were excellent (often covering the many and varied ways of taking down a target) but then there were the collector hobbyist's busywork challenges!  Basically, these amounted to finding a massive inventory of objects in each chapter.  You can spend far too much time picking up and dropping bottles, bricks, ornaments, wrenches, hammers, the occasional mannequin arm or a dog bone(!) - you name it, you need to grab it for the 'find' to be registered - only to get to the end and find you missed a whole load more.  It reached the point where Agent 47 was leaving quite a trail of broken and dropped debris behind him (hardly stealthy) and it broke the whole role-playing vibe (I felt more like an antiques vs junk collector vs home-wrecker rather than deadly assassin)!  Why even bother doing it then?  The problem is that the game informs you that you only completed, say, 17 out of 40 achievements.  You might have achieved all the important ones (the assassination hits and such), but such a low number results from not being a kleptomaniac and leaves a less than satisfied feeling for the completionist type of gamer.

Finally, the story didn't really go anywhere.  It started out okay, but never really warmed up.  It was 'acceptable' in that it at least had a story unlike (polite cough) [i]Thief 2014[/i], but the whole thing really built up to - well, nothing!  I can't really say much without going into spoilers, but let's say that the final epilogue is a huge disappointment when compared to the earlier strong gameplay and was over all too easily - with the final expected 'boss fight' completely removed from the player's hands.   

[h1]And the summary...[/h1]
Despite those horrid points of no return, [i]Hitman Absolution[/i] is a strong contender in the stealth genre.  It's at its best when played as intended: as a secret and silent assassin.  You can go in all guns blazing but it won't be the same satisfying experience.  If you didn't enjoy Blood Money, don't write this one off - especially if you've enjoyed games like [i]Dishonored[/i] or the [i]Thief[/i] franchise.  Definitely recommended!

Hitman: Absolution takes Agent 47 into a more personal and cinematic adventure than many of his traditional assignments. Developed by IO Interactive and published by IO Interactive on its current Steam release, the game follows the legendary assassin after circumstances force him to turn against the organization he once served. His decision to protect a mysterious young woman named Victoria places him in conflict with the Agency and a collection of dangerous criminals. The story provides a stronger narrative thread between missions, creating an experience that feels like a stealth-action thriller rather than simply a sequence of unrelated assassination contracts.

Stealth remains the foundation of the gameplay. Agent 47 enters environments filled with guards, civilians, potential witnesses, useful objects, alternate routes, and opportunities for deception. Players can sneak through restricted areas, distract enemies, hide bodies, incapacitate opponents, acquire disguises, or search for environmental methods of eliminating targets. Rushing directly toward an objective is rarely as rewarding as observing the surroundings first. Learning patrol patterns and discovering weaknesses can turn an apparently difficult situation into a remarkably clean infiltration.

The disguise system is especially important. Taking another character's clothing can provide access to areas that would normally be dangerous, but disguises do not automatically make 47 invisible. Certain characters can recognize someone who does not belong, forcing the player to avoid close inspection or use Instinct to blend in. This makes disguises useful without completely removing the tension from restricted locations. Instinct can also highlight important characters and environmental information, giving players a clearer understanding of their surroundings.

Although stealth produces some of the most satisfying moments, Absolution also provides capable third-person combat. Pistols, shotguns, rifles, melee weapons, and improvised objects give 47 plenty of options when a carefully prepared plan collapses. Shooting is responsive and appropriately powerful, while the Point Shooting mechanic reinforces 47's reputation as an exceptionally skilled marksman. Going loud can be entertaining, but it usually removes much of the strategic satisfaction that comes from completing an area without raising an alarm.

Mission design is where Absolution differs most noticeably from the sandbox-oriented philosophy commonly associated with Hitman. Many areas are relatively contained, and the campaign frequently moves 47 through a succession of smaller environments rather than consistently providing enormous assassination playgrounds. Some objectives are primarily about reaching an exit or escaping hostile territory. This structure improves narrative pacing and keeps the campaign moving, but it can occasionally make the player feel more restricted than expected.

Fortunately, many locations still contain considerable room for experimentation. Alternative paths, disguises, accidents, hidden equipment, environmental interactions, and optional challenges encourage repeat attempts. A messy first playthrough can become dramatically different once the player understands the layout. Returning to a mission with knowledge of guard routes and useful disguises can transform a stressful infiltration into a smooth professional operation. The scoring system further encourages efficient play by rewarding restraint and skill while discouraging unnecessary casualties.

Presentation remains one of the game's strongest qualities. Its environments have a gritty and sometimes oppressive visual character, supported by detailed interiors, atmospheric lighting, large crowds, and numerous background activities. Streets, buildings, clubs, industrial areas, and public spaces feel convincingly populated. Civilian conversations and guard dialogue also add personality to locations while occasionally providing clues about possible routes or opportunities.

The story adopts a deliberately dark and exaggerated tone. Villains are frequently grotesque, violent, and larger than life, while the campaign contains plenty of mature themes and brutal situations. This approach will not appeal equally to everyone, particularly because the writing sometimes pushes its characters toward caricature. Nevertheless, it gives the campaign a distinctive identity. Agent 47 remains controlled and intimidating throughout, while his responsibility toward Victoria allows the narrative to explore a slightly more human side of the normally detached assassin.

Replay value is substantial for players interested in improving their performance. Challenges, achievements, different assassination techniques, alternative routes, weapon discoveries, and higher scores provide reasons to revisit missions. Experimenting with stealth, disguises, environmental kills, and direct combat reveals how many systems are operating beneath the cinematic presentation. Players interested only in completing the storyline may experience a fairly straightforward campaign, while completionists can spend considerably longer mastering individual stages.

On Steam Deck, Hitman: Absolution is officially listed as Playable rather than fully Verified. The game can run on the handheld and is practical to play with its controller-oriented gameplay, but users may encounter minor compatibility considerations that prevent it from receiving the highest Deck certification. Given the game's age and relatively modest PC requirements, it remains an appealing portable option for players willing to accept those limitations.

Hitman: Absolution is ultimately a strong stealth-action game that takes a more directed approach to Agent 47's profession. Its atmospheric environments, flexible infiltration mechanics, satisfying disguises, environmental assassinations, competent combat, and excellent presentation remain enjoyable despite the more linear campaign design. Players looking specifically for enormous unrestricted assassination sandboxes may find portions of the campaign limiting, but those comfortable with a combination of cinematic storytelling and methodical stealth will find plenty to appreciate. It may not represent the most open-ended interpretation of Hitman, but it remains a polished, memorable, and highly replayable chapter in Agent 47's career.

A "meh" recommendation. Ever play a game that just drips with high production values and class, but you still don't like it? That's how I feel about Hitman: Absolution. I realize that it's something plenty of people will enjoy. I just didn't. Do I think it's worth picking up? Sure, if it's on sale. And you're bored.

If that sounds like I'm getting ready to drop some grade-A hate, I'm not. At least, I don't want to. There is so much about Hitman: Absolution that just reeks of care and attention. The graphics are amazing. Not necessarily a reason to buy a game, but they are. The voice acting is superb (Keith Carradine and Powers Boothe? Hell yes!). The soundtrack works incredibly well, giving an almost Bond-esque ambiance without ever getting too loud. While some levels are occasionally re-used, there are a lot of different locations and settings. And as far as the story goes, I felt incredibly close to Agent 47 (he's quite sympathetic, despite his stoicism). Sneaking from cover to cover feels fluid and natural. Weapons are deadly (headshots are a breeze with the Silverballers). 

So what's my problem?
Most of the levels are claustrophobic (the opening Chinatown level and the cornfield level are exceptions). The paths through the levels are restrictive. And some levels don't even bother to hide their linearity (final rooftop level, among many others). There's no way to level-up Agent 47. Upgrades are unlocked based upon how high of a score you received upon completing a mission. But the points system clearly favors a specific path – even penalizing for non-target knockouts. I was never a fan of the Assassin's Creed games' “full synchonization” mechanic either, but this just ticked me off. There is no loadout customization; you start every mission with choke-wire and (after you unlock them) the Silverballers. Other weapons are acquired by finding them or picking them up from dead enemies – but it doesn't matter, because you'll be back to the piano wire and Silverballers once the next mission starts.
 
Disguises are actually not a problem; there are plenty of them around. Using them is sometimes strange, though. If planning to ghost through a police station, DON'T try to use a police uniform as a disguise. Why? Because if a cop gets too close to you, he'll detect that you're not a real policeman. Makes sense, I suppose. But in a level crawling with police, disguising as a police officer becomes a questionable strategy – which seems counter-intuitive to me. Much better to knock out a homeless person and take his disguise, since the officers won't detect you. But then, dressed as a homeless person, you won't be able to enter restricted areas without attracting attention anyway. Several times I just lost patience and started taking innocent people out to facilitate progress – and several times got embroiled in a full-on gun battle. Which actually wasn't that bad. If you're careful, 47 has a ton of health, and headshots are 1-hit kills. Add in the deadly Instinct combat mode, which has elements of the VATS system from Fallout, and 47 becomes an absolute wrecking ball of death.

There were some great moments, though. Ghosting through the flaming warehouse while troopers searched the premises was a thrill. Heading deeper underground through a mining facility with guards everywhere was a delicate game of cat-and-mouse. And trying to take out three henchmen in Chinatown with throngs of people everywhere was easily the most enjoyment I had. Somehow I thought every level would feature that amount of variety and detail, and I'm disappointed that (to me) it didn't. Recommended because Hitman: Absolution is polished and does what it sets out to do, but ultimately it's only a mediocre game that is sprinkled with some great levels.
